questions.prompt: Why do wrong answers from an LLM usually sound just as confident as right ones?

options.text: The model is trained to deceive users
Confident phrasing is the most likely continuation style in its training text, produced the same way whether the fact is right or invented
The model is always at least 90% sure of what it says
Wrong answers actually do sound noticeably more hesitant

questions.explanation: Training text — articles, textbooks, explanations — overwhelmingly sounds sure of itself, so confident tone is simply the likeliest style to predict. Tone is part of the output, not a self-report of certainty. There's no deception motive (a) and no reliable hesitancy signal (d).

questions.prompt: Which situations call for verifying the model's answer before acting on it? Select all that apply.

options.text: It suggested a medication dosage for your child
It brainstormed 20 names for your book club
It stated a statistic you're about to put in a presentation
It gave you a deadline for a government form you must file
It drafted a silly birthday poem

questions.explanation: Dosages and filing deadlines are high-stakes (and for medical questions, AI should only assist a professional or primary source, never replace one); a statistic you'll repeat publicly is medium-stakes and worth checking. Brainstormed names (b) and a poem (e) are low-stakes — usefulness is the only test, so verification adds nothing.

questions.prompt: You ask the same factual question in two fresh conversations and get confident but CONTRADICTORY answers. What should you conclude?

options.text: The first answer is right because it came first
At least one confident answer is wrong — treat the fact as unverified and check a real source
The longer, more detailed answer is the correct one

questions.explanation: Contradiction under reruns is a hallucination red flag: the model is sampling plausible-sounding answers, not retrieving a solid fact. Order (a), averaging (c), and length or detail (d) carry no evidence — detail is generated as fluently as everything else. Go to a primary source.

questions.prompt: Which is the best use of the 'trust / verify / wrong-tool' rule?

options.text: Trust everything from the model that sounds professional
Verify every single output no matter how trivial, or don't use AI at all
Match your checking effort to the stakes: use drafts freely, verify facts you'll rely on, and keep AI as assistant-only for medical, legal, and financial decisions
Only use AI for questions you already know the answer to

questions.explanation: Stakes-based checking is the working professional's approach: it keeps the speed benefits for low-stakes work while protecting you where errors are costly. Blanket trust (a) ignores everything this lesson showed; blanket verification (b) or only-known-answers (d) throws away most of the tool's value.
